html:
The oldest institution of higher learning in the United States, founded in 1636 by vote of the General Court of the Massachusetts Bay Colony, in a town soon renamed Cambridge. It was named in 1639 for John Harvard, a young Puritan minister who left it his library and half his estate.

The Puritan settlers had arrived only six years before. They wanted an educated ministry and feared, in their own words, leaving an "illiterate ministry to the churches" when their pastors died. The early college taught Latin, Greek, Hebrew, logic and divinity, on the model of Cambridge in England, where many of the founders had studied. The colony's first printing press was set up nearby in 1638. In the 1650s Harvard even had an Indian College, where a few Native students studied.

Harvard grew into a university with schools of medicine, law and more, and into one of the richest and most influential universities in the world. Eight US presidents graduated from it.
